entries.title: Cooling stocks and sauces
entries.say: As it reads: cooling stocks and sauces.
entries.summary: Cooked food that will be kept must lose its heat quickly, in two timed stages, so the bacteria that survive cooking never get the warm hours they need. Big, thick pots need the most help.
entries.guest: How the kitchen makes and keeps its soups and sauces is the chef's to answer, so let me ask and come straight back to you.

paras: Cooling is the stretch between the stove and the fridge, where big batches most often go wrong. Cooking kills most bacteria but not all: Clostridium perfringens and Bacillus cereus form spores, tough resting cells that survive the boil and wake as the food cools. In a deep pot that cools slowly they multiply through the warm hours, and a stock or a pot of beans that looked fine can make a dining room ill.

The FDA Food Code, the model behind most American health codes, calls such foods TCS, short for time and temperature control for safety: stocks, sauces, soups, cooked rice, beans and meat. Cooling is a clock nobody can see on the plate, so it is timed, probed and written down.

The Food Code sets two stages. First, from 57°C (135°F) to 21°C (70°F) within 2 hours. Then on to 5°C (41°F) or below within a total of 6 hours, so if the first stage takes its full 2 hours, 4 hours remain for the second. The first stage has the shorter clock because it covers the range where bacteria grow quickest. These figures are the 2022 Food Code's; FDA issued a new edition on 17 September 2026 that adds an alternative cooling process, and the kitchen follows its own health authority's code and its written procedure.

Heat leaves through surfaces, so every tool gives the food more surface or more cold. Stand the pot in an ice bath, ice and water up to the level of the food, and stir: stirring carries hot liquid from the middle to the cold wall. An ice wand, a sealed paddle of frozen water, is stirred through the pot. Pour thick food into shallow metal pans, about 5 cm (2 inches) deep, and divide big batches. A blast chiller does the same work with fast, cold air, and where the recipe allows, ice can stand in for some of the water.

In the walk-in, cooling pans sit uncovered or loosely covered on a top shelf, with air around them and nothing stacked on top; a tight lid traps the heat. Probe the centre about every hour, so a slow pan is caught in time, and log each reading with its time. If the food is still above 21°C (70°F) at 2 hours, tell the chef at once; the written procedure decides whether it is reheated and cooled again or discarded.

Thin stock cools fastest because it circulates, carrying heat to the cold wall. Thick food barely moves, so heat has to creep out through the food itself. Gumbo, roux-thickened sauces such as velouté and espagnole, red beans, rice and braises can keep a warm core for hours in a deep pot. They need the most care: shallow pans at once, frequent stirring and the probe in the centre, never at the edge.

Never put a full, hot stockpot straight into the walk-in. A walk-in holds cold food cold; it is not built to pull the heat out of 20 litres (about 5 gallons) of stock. The pot warms the air and everything near it, the cream and the raw fish included, while its own centre stays warm far into the night.

Cooled food wanted hot again is reheated quickly on the stove or in the oven, never in the steam table, until every part reaches 74°C (165°F) for 15 seconds, within 2 hours. Every container in the walk-in is labelled with what it is, the date and time it was made and the cook's initials. Ready-to-eat food kept longer than 24 hours is also marked with its last day, at most 7 days at 5°C (41°F) or below, with the day of making counted as the first.

Most cooling failures are quiet: a pot left on the range to cool a little loses its first hour, a lid traps the heat, the ice melts unnoticed, a warm core goes unprobed. A stock that smells sour or looks cloudy and fizzy has cooled too slowly or been kept too long. It is thrown away, never boiled again in hope: boiling does not undo the toxins some bacteria have already made.

A server never sees the cooling, but its questions reach the table: was the soup made today, has it been reheated? Never guess; take the question to the kitchen. Out front, a lukewarm soup goes back, and an unlabelled container in a side station goes to the chef.

faults.fault: The centre is still warm the next morning
faults.cause: A deep pot or a full container went into the walk-in, so the core never lost its heat.
faults.fix: Divide hot food into shallow pans in an ice bath straight off the stove, probe the centre and log each reading.

faults.fault: The walk-in reads warm during prep
faults.cause: Hot pots were put inside to cool, warming the air and everything around them.
faults.fix: Cool hot food in an ice bath or a blast chiller first, and move it to the walk-in in shallow pans.

faults.fault: The ice bath has turned to warm water
faults.cause: Too little ice, or the melt was never topped up.
faults.fix: Drain some water, add fresh ice, keep the level up to the food line and stir every few minutes.

faults.fault: Stock smells sour or looks cloudy and fizzy
faults.cause: It cooled too slowly or was kept too long, and bacteria grew in it.
faults.fix: Throw it away. Boiling again does not undo the toxins some bacteria have already made.

faults.fault: A container in the walk-in has no label
faults.cause: It was meant to be labelled later, and never was.
faults.fix: If nobody can say what it is and when it was made, it is discarded. Label before it goes in.

(B) TIME/TEMPERATURE CONTROL FOR SAFETY FOOD shall be cooled within 4 hours to 5°C (41°F) or less if prepared from ingredients at ambient temperature, such as reconstituted FOODS and canned tuna. 3-501.15 Cooling Methods. (A) ... (1) Placing the FOOD in shallow pans; (2) Separating the FOOD into smaller or thinner portions; (3) Using rapid cooling EQUIPMENT; (4) Stirring the FOOD in a container placed in an ice water bath; (5) Using containers that facilitate heat transfer; (6) Adding ice as an ingredient; or (7) Other effective methods. (B) ... FOOD containers in which FOOD is being cooled shall be ... Arranged in the EQUIPMENT to provide maximum heat transfer through the container walls; and ... Loosely covered, or uncovered if protected from overhead contamination ... 3-403.11 ... cooked and cooled TIME/TEMPERATURE CONTROL FOR SAFETY FOOD that is reheated for hot holding shall be reheated so that all parts of the FOOD reach a temperature of at least 74°C (165°F) for 15 seconds. ... entries.title: The danger zone and hot holding
entries.say: As it reads: the danger zone and hot holding.
entries.summary: The danger zone is 5 to 57°C (41 to 135°F), where bacteria multiply fastest. Food is held above or below it, checked with a calibrated thermometer, or kept on a written clock and served or thrown away by its marked time.
entries.guest: Hot dishes go out hot and cold dishes cold; if anything reaches you lukewarm, please tell me and I will take it straight back to the kitchen.

paras: The danger zone is the band of temperatures in which the bacteria that make people ill multiply fastest. The FDA Food Code, the model behind most American health codes, sets its edges through its holding rules: 5 to 57°C (41 to 135°F). Cold below it slows most bacteria to a crawl; heat above it stops them growing. The USDA notes that in its own, slightly wider band bacteria can double in number in as little as 20 minutes, so a pan left out all afternoon can turn a few hundred cells into millions.

The Food Code figures in this entry come from its 2022 edition; FDA issued a new edition on 17 September 2026, and a kitchen works to the code its own authority has adopted, so learn the house's numbers. The rule is simple: food is kept hot, kept cold or kept on a written clock, and it passes through the zone as quickly as it can.

Hot holding means cooked food kept at 57°C (135°F) or above until it is served; cold holding means 5°C (41°F) or below. Steam tables, bains-marie (pans of hot water in which containers of sauce stand to keep warm), soup wells and warming drawers hold hot food; the fridge, the walk-in and the cold rail, the chilled well of containers on the line, hold cold. Keep lids on, stir soups and sauces so the top does not cool, keep the water topped up, and take the food's own temperature: the unit's dial reads the water or the air, not the sauce.

Steam tables and bains-marie hold heat; they are not built to raise it. Cooled food set in a steam table climbs through the zone far too slowly, so it is reheated first, on the stove or in the oven, until every part reaches 74°C (165°F). The cold side works the same way: a cold rail keeps chilled food cold, it does not chill warm food.

Use the thermometer every time: stir, push the probe into the thickest part or the centre of the pan, wait for the reading to settle and write it on the log. Clean and sanitise the probe between foods so it never carries raw juices into cooked food. Calibrate it at the start of each shift and after any knock: in a glass packed with crushed ice and topped with water, it should read the freezing point of water; if not, adjust it or take it out of use. The Food Code asks for accuracy within one degree Celsius, or two Fahrenheit.

Some kitchens use a written exception called time as a public health control: instead of holding a food hot or cold, they hold it on a clock. Under the Food Code the food starts at 5°C (41°F) or below, or at 57°C (135°F) or above, and is marked with the time 4 hours after it left temperature control. Within those 4 hours it is served or thrown away. It never goes back into the fridge or the hot well to reset the clock, and an unmarked container is discarded.

A second form allows up to 6 hours for cold food that starts at 5°C (41°F) or below and never rises above 21°C (70°F). Either way the procedure is written in advance, kept in the kitchen and shown to the health inspector on request, and the cook follows it, not memory.

Holding fails in small, ordinary ways: a soup well with its water run dry, a sauce judged by the dial, a pan left on the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, between rushes, a thermometer not calibrated since it fell, a cold rail packed above its fill line so the top layer sits in warm air. Each has the same cure, a probe in the food and a reading on the log, and a wrong reading goes straight to the chef.

Servers hold food too: at the pass, at the tray stand, a folding rack for a loaded tray, and at the side station, the servers' stand in the dining room. Run plates as soon as they are up, keep cold garnishes and butter in the cold, and never park a plate under a heat lamp for a table that is not ready. A guest who says a dish is lukewarm is thanked, and the plate goes back to the kitchen for the chef to decide.

entries.title: Cooking temperatures and the consumer advisory
entries.say: As it reads: cooking temperatures and the consumer advisory.
entries.summary: The Food Code sets a minimum internal temperature and time for each raw animal food. Learn the figures, probe the thickest part, and know why a seared whole steak may be served rare, and why tartare and rosy duck call for the consumer advisory.
entries.guest: How would you like your steak cooked? The note on the menu covers raw and undercooked dishes, and I am glad to take any question about it to the chef.

paras: Cooking kills the bacteria raw animal food carries, by temperature and time together: the hotter the food, the shorter the hold it needs. The FDA Food Code sets each food a minimum internal temperature and a time to hold it there. Poultry, and stuffed meat, fish and pasta, go to 74°C (165°F) for an instant, less than 1 second. Minced meat goes to 68°C (155°F) for 17 seconds. Fish and whole cuts of meat, such as steaks and chops, go to 63°C (145°F) for 15 seconds.

Minced meat shows the trade between heat and time: the code also accepts 63°C (145°F) for 3 minutes, 66°C (150°F) for 1 minute or 70°C (158°F) for an instant. Older editions, still followed by some local codes, asked a longer hold for poultry, and charts for home cooks differ. The figures here are the 2022 Food Code's; FDA issued a new edition on 17 September 2026, and a kitchen works to its local code and its own written standard.

Probe the thickest part, away from bone, fat and the pan, and check two spots on an irregular piece. For thin foods such as fish fillets, push a thin-tipped probe in from the side so the tip sits at the centre, and wait for the reading to settle. Use a calibrated thermometer, sanitised between foods.

Meat goes on cooking after it leaves the heat: the hot outside keeps warming the cooler centre as it rests, a few degrees in a steak and more in a large roast. Cooks use this carryover to land a doneness, pulling the meat a little early. Where a dish has to meet a minimum, though, the reading that counts is the one you take: probe again after the rest.

Why may a steak be served rare when minced beef may not? In a whole, intact muscle the bacteria sit on the surface and the inside is protected, so a good sear deals with them. The Food Code lets a whole-muscle, intact beef steak, labelled as such by its supplier, be served rare, outside places that serve highly susceptible groups such as hospitals and care homes, when top and bottom reach a surface temperature of 63°C (145°F) or above and every outside surface shows a cooked change of colour.

Mincing spreads the surface through the whole batch, and a needle-tenderised or injected steak has had its surface pushed inside, so their centres must be cooked. Stuffing soaks up raw juices and sits at the coolest heart of the dish, which is why stuffed foods take the poultry figure.

Some dishes are raw or undercooked by design: steak tartare, a rosy duck breast, an egg with a runny yolk, oysters on the half shell. The code allows them when the guest asks for or chooses them, outside places that serve highly susceptible groups, provided the guest is told through the consumer advisory, and never undercooked minced meat from a children's menu.

The advisory has two parts. The disclosure marks the dish, with a plain description such as oysters on the half shell (raw oysters) or an asterisk to a footnote saying it is served raw or undercooked. The reminder is the warning, in words such as: consuming raw or undercooked meats, poultry, seafood, shellfish or eggs may increase your risk of foodborne illness, and the kitchen answers any question it raises. It matters most to young children, older people, anyone pregnant and anyone whose immune system is weakened.

Three Brennan's dishes show the rules. The Steak Tartare Cannoli is raw beef tartare in a crisp potato shell with a grated cured egg yolk, and its service note marks it for the consumer advisory. The Roasted Rohan Duck Breast on the dinner tasting is served rosy, usually medium-rare to medium: confirm the kitchen's standard at lineup. Whether our menu marks the duck for the advisory is confirmed at lineup too. The Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak is at its best medium-rare to medium; always ask the temperature and write it on the ticket.

At the table, ask the doneness of every steak, duck breast and burger, and write it on the ticket. If a guest asks whether rare or raw is risky, neither reassure nor frighten: point to the note on the menu, say the chef can answer, and bring the answer back. Never promise an outcome, and never change the doneness a guest chose without asking.

faults.fault: The reading was taken near the surface or the bone
faults.cause: The probe tip never reached the thickest part.
faults.fix: Push the tip into the centre of the thickest part, from the side for thin pieces, and check a second spot.

faults.cause: The meat was pulled early in the hope that carryover would finish it.
faults.fix: Probe after the rest and return it to the heat until it reaches its figure.

faults.fault: The thermometer reads several degrees out
faults.cause: It was knocked and not calibrated again.
faults.fix: Calibrate it in iced water, and take it out of use if it cannot be adjusted.

faults.fault: Raw juices carried into cooked food
faults.cause: The probe was not cleaned between items.
faults.fix: Wipe and sanitise the probe after every reading.

sources.evidence: 3-401.11 (A) ... (1) 63°C (145°F) or above for 15 seconds for: ... FISH, MEAT, and commercially raised GAME ANIMALS. (2) 68°C (155°F) for 17 seconds or the temperature specified in the following chart that corresponds to the holding time for ... the following if they are COMMINUTED: FISH, MEAT, GAME ANIMALS commercially raised for FOOD ... Minimum Temperature °C (°F), Time: 63 (145) 3 minutes; 66 (150) 1 minute; 70 (158) < 1 second (instantaneous) ... (3) 74°C (165°F) ... < 1 second (instantaneous) for POULTRY, BALUTS, wild GAME ANIMALS ..., stuffed FISH, stuffed MEAT, stuffed pasta, stuffed POULTRY, stuffed RATITES, or stuffing containing FISH, MEAT, POULTRY, or RATITES. (C) A raw or undercooked whole-muscle, intact beef steak may be served or offered for sale in a READY-TO-EAT form if: (1) The FOOD ESTABLISHMENT serves a population that is not a HIGHLY SUSCEPTIBLE POPULATION, (2) The steak is labeled to indicate that it meets the definition of "whole-muscle, intact beef" as specified under ¶ 3-201.11(E), and (3) The steak is cooked on both the top and bottom to a surface temperature of 63°C (145°F) or above and a cooked color change is achieved on all external surfaces. (D) A raw animal FOOD such as raw EGG, raw FISH, raw-marinated FISH, raw MOLLUSCAN SHELLFISH, or steak tartare; or a partially cooked FOOD such as lightly cooked FISH, soft cooked EGGS, or rare MEAT other than whole-muscle, intact beef steaks ... may be served or offered for sale upon CONSUMER request or selection in a READY-TO-EAT form if: (1) ... the FOOD ESTABLISHMENT serves a population that is not a HIGHLY SUSCEPTIBLE POPULATION; (2) The FOOD, if served or offered for service by CONSUMER selection from a children's menu, does not contain COMMINUTED MEAT; and ... The CONSUMER is informed as specified under § 3-603.11 ... 3-603.11 ... DISCLOSURE shall include: ... A description of the animal-derived FOODS, such as "oysters on the half shell (raw oysters)," ... or ... Identification of the animal-derived FOODS by asterisking them to a footnote that states that the items are served raw or undercooked, or contain (or may contain) raw or undercooked ingredients. ... REMINDER ... Consuming raw or undercooked MEATS, POULTRY, SEAFOOD, SHELLFISH, or EGGS may increase your RISK of foodborne illness; or ... Consuming raw or undercooked MEATS, POULTRY, SEAFOOD, SHELLFISH, or EGGS may increase your RISK of foodborne illness, especially if you have certain medical conditions.

cards.front: What is the Food Code's minimum for poultry?
cards.back: 74°C (165°F) for an instant, less than 1 second, read at the thickest part; stuffed meat, fish and pasta take the same figure.

cards.front: What is the Food Code's minimum for minced meat, and why is it higher than for steak?
cards.back: 68°C (155°F) for 17 seconds, or a hotter figure for less time: mincing spreads surface bacteria through the whole batch.

cards.front: What is the Food Code's minimum for fish and whole cuts of meat?
cards.back: 63°C (145°F) for 15 seconds at the thickest part, unless the guest chooses it less cooked, as the code allows.

cards.front: Where do you probe a piece of meat or fish?
cards.back: In the thickest part, away from bone, fat and the pan, from the side for thin pieces, and in more than one spot on an irregular piece.

cards.front: What is carryover, and how does it bear on a minimum temperature?
cards.back: The rise in the centre as meat rests. Use it to land a doneness, but where a minimum applies, probe again after the rest.

cards.front: Why may a whole steak be served rare when minced beef is cooked through?
cards.back: In an intact muscle the bacteria sit on the surface, which the sear deals with; mincing spreads them through the meat.

cards.front: What must a rare whole-muscle steak have under the Food Code?
cards.back: A surface of 63°C (145°F) or above on top and bottom and a cooked change of colour on every outside surface.

cards.front: Why are stuffed foods cooked to the poultry figure?
cards.back: The stuffing soaks up raw juices and sits at the coolest heart of the dish, so it needs 74°C (165°F).

cards.front: What are the two parts of the consumer advisory?
cards.back: The disclosure, which describes the dish or asterisks it to a footnote, and the reminder, the warning that raw or undercooked food may increase risk.

cards.front: Where may raw or undercooked food never be served, even when a guest asks?
cards.back: In places that serve highly susceptible groups, such as hospitals and care homes; and undercooked minced meat is never served from a children's menu.

cards.front: A guest asks whether a rare steak is risky. What do you say?
cards.back: Point to the note on the menu and say the chef can answer, then bring back the answer; never reassure and never promise an outcome.

cards.front: Which Brennan's dish does the service note mark for the consumer advisory as raw beef?
cards.back: The Steak Tartare Cannoli: raw beef tartare in a crisp potato shell with a grated cured egg yolk. Send questions to the kitchen.

questions.q: What minimum does the Food Code set for a chicken breast?
questions.answer: 74°C (165°F) for an instant
distractors: 63°C (145°F) for 15 seconds
57°C (135°F) for 1 minute
54°C (130°F) for 10 minutes
questions.why: Poultry takes the highest figure, 74°C (165°F), and the current code asks no hold beyond an instant, less than 1 second; stuffed foods share it.

questions.q: Which figure does the Food Code give for minced beef?
questions.answer: 68°C (155°F) for 17 seconds
distractors: 63°C (145°F) for 15 seconds
54°C (130°F) for 1 second
60°C (140°F) for 5 seconds
questions.why: Mincing carries surface bacteria into the centre, so minced meat needs more than a whole cut: 68°C (155°F) for 17 seconds.

questions.q: Which foods share the Food Code's minimum of 63°C (145°F) for 15 seconds?
questions.answer: Fish and whole cuts of meat
distractors: Poultry and stuffing
Minced beef and sausage
Stuffed pasta and stuffed fish
questions.why: The code gives fish and intact whole cuts the lower figure; poultry, minced meat and stuffed foods need higher ones.

questions.q: Where should the probe go in a thick pork chop?
questions.answer: The thickest part, away from the bone
distractors: Right beside the bone, where it is thickest
Just under the surface, where it browns
Into the fat at the edge, the last to heat
questions.why: Bone, fat and the surface all read differently from the meat; the thickest part is the last to heat.

questions.q: A roast is pulled early to allow for carryover and must meet a minimum. What should the cook do?
questions.answer: Probe again after the rest
distractors: Assume carryover did the work
Slice it at once to stop the cooking
Serve it and note the time
questions.why: Carryover helps land a doneness, but where a minimum applies, only a reading taken after the rest shows it was met.

questions.q: Why can a whole-muscle steak be served rare while minced beef is cooked through?
questions.answer: Its bacteria sit on the surface the sear reaches
distractors: The sear's heat reaches right to its centre
Ageing the steak kills its bacteria
Minced beef comes from older, tougher animals
questions.why: An intact muscle keeps its bacteria on the outside; mincing, needling or injecting carries them into the centre.

questions.q: To what figure is a stuffed fish cooked under the Food Code?
questions.why: Stuffing soaks up raw juices and sits at the coolest centre, so stuffed foods take the poultry figure.

questions.q: What does the reminder part of the consumer advisory tell guests?
questions.answer: Raw or undercooked food may raise the risk of illness
distractors: Which dishes are served at room temperature
That the kitchen guarantees every dish it serves
How long each dish takes to cook to order
questions.why: The disclosure marks the dish; the reminder is the warning that eating it raw or undercooked may increase risk.

questions.q: Which undercooked dish may never be served from a children's menu, even on request?
questions.answer: A burger cooked pink in the middle
distractors: A whole steak seared and served rare
A soft-cooked egg with a runny yolk
Seared tuna left rare at the centre
questions.why: The code bars undercooked minced meat from a children's menu outright, because mincing carries surface bacteria to the centre; the other dishes go under the advisory.

questions.q: A guest asks whether the Steak Tartare Cannoli is risky for her. What does the server do?
questions.answer: Point to the advisory, then ask the kitchen
distractors: Reassure her that the beef is bought very fresh
Explain the risks of raw beef in detail yourself
Steer her to another starter without saying why
questions.why: A server never promises an outcome; the advisory informs the guest and the kitchen answers the risk question.
